w: Opened by Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother on 16 July 1957 as the National Gallery of Rhodesia, designed and directed by Frank McEwen, who brought Shona stone sculpture to world attention. Queen Elizabeth II attended its sixth Heritage Exhibition in 1991. It holds stone, metal and wood sculpture, plus paintings.
s: Where Shona sculpture found world fame
_facts: Opened 16 July 1957 as the National Gallery of Rhodesia
Designed and directed by Frank McEwen, who championed Shona sculpture
Queen Elizabeth II attended its sixth Zimbabwe Heritage Exhibition in 1991
Current executive director is Raphael Chikukwa

w: Fifteen acres of landscaped gardens in the Msasa suburb, given over entirely to the work of Zimbabwean stone sculptors. The park showcases the country's tradition of African stone sculpture, the same movement of Shona carving that Harare's National Gallery helped bring to attention decades earlier.
s: 15 acres devoted to Zimbabwean stone carving
_facts: Sculpture garden in the Msasa suburb of Harare
Spans over 15 acres of landscaped gardens
Dedicated to showcasing African stone sculpture heritage

w: A 23-hectare hilltop burial ground seven kilometres from Harare, honouring Patriotic Front guerrillas killed in the Bush War and Zimbabweans since judged to merit hero status. Its monument is shaped like two AK-47s back to back, graves arranged like the magazines, built by North Korea's Mansudae Overseas Projects.
s: Monument shaped like two crossed AK-47s
_facts: 23-hectare site, 7km from central Harare

Monument modelled on two AK-47s laid back to back
Built by North Korean firm Mansudae Overseas Projects

w: Established by an Act of Parliament in 1935, the archives once served as the central repository for the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, from 1953 to 1963. Holdings include 15,000 audiovisual items and an Oral History Programme, plus a Community Archives Project begun in 2018.
s: Regional archive since 1935, oral history too

w: A mansion built in 2006 by the ruling ZANU-PF party as a family home for then-president Robert Mugabe, in the Borrowdale suburb, nicknamed simply for the colour of its roof. Ownership passed to the Mugabe family after his death, leaving one of Harare's most recognisable private addresses.

Located in the Borrowdale suburb

n: Cathedral of St Mary and All Saints, Harare
w: An Anglican cathedral begun in 1913 to designs by British architect Herbert Baker, who also designed the cathedrals of Cape Town and Johannesburg. It stands at the intersection of Nelson Mandela Avenue and Sam Nujoma Street, a colonial-era design linking Harare's cathedral to two other southern African cities.
